messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Vignette:
Mele was a 61-year-old security guard of Pacific Islander heritage who had lived alone for years and had always prided herself on being dependable, calm in a crisis, and careful with people. That sense of herself was shaken one winter evening when, while working at a large office complex, she accidentally caused a serious injury to another person during a routine incident in the building’s parking area. She spoke of the moment in fragments: the sudden movement, the confusion, the shock of realizing immediately that something had gone terribly wrong. Even now, parts of that night remained inaccessible to her no matter how many times she tried to replay it. She would say, with visible frustration, that there were “blank pieces” she could not recover, as though her mind had sealed off sections of the scene. What she did remember felt strangely detached, almost like a report about someone else’s life. At times she could describe the sequence of events in plain detail, but without feeling, as if she were recounting an incident that had happened to a stranger rather than to her own body and hands.

In the weeks that followed, Mele found herself repeatedly turning the event over in her mind, trying to understand how an ordinary shift had ended in such harm. She spent long stretches thinking about why it had happened to her, returning again and again to the same questions: what she had missed, what she had done wrong, whether there had been some moment when she could have acted differently. She dwelled on the event with a punishing intensity, not in a single orderly recollection but in a jagged cycle of self-questioning. She would sit at her kitchen table after work, staring into her tea, and mentally reconstruct the night step by step, then start over because she still could not make the details fit together. The more she tried to make sense of it, the more she focused on the fragments she could not retrieve, and the more unsettled she became by the feeling that something essential was missing.

At work, those missing pieces and the sense that the memory belonged to someone else made it hard for her to trust her own recollection of what had happened. The office complex where she was employed remained the same place she had to return to, with its parking area, its corridors, and the ordinary evening routines of staff and visitors. Walking that route on shift, she found herself pulled back toward the scene in a way she did not choose. Sometimes, when she passed the area where the incident occurred, she would stop and stare without really seeing it, her mind trying and failing to line up the remembered facts. She did not describe herself as refusing to go to work, but she began to approach the building differently, lingering before entering, taking longer routes within her post, and quietly trying to keep herself away from the exact spot where the event had unfolded. Over time, this changed how she carried out her job. She became more preoccupied during shifts and less comfortable being alone with her thoughts during the quieter hours of the evening. Coworkers noticed that she seemed withdrawn, and Mele herself admitted that the sense of distance she felt from the memory made her uneasy, as though she could not fully trust what her own mind was showing her.

What troubled her most was the moral weight she placed on the event. She had come to believe that there must be some reason this had happened to her, and she searched for that reason with painful persistence. Being someone who had spent her life trying to do things properly, she could not stop returning to what she saw as her own failure. She went over the details endlessly, sometimes aloud, sometimes silently, trying to identify the exact point at which she had gone wrong. There were moments when she felt numb as she recalled the incident, unable to connect emotionally to the facts she recited; at other moments, the same facts struck her with a cold sense of personal wrongdoing. The result was a life narrowed by repetition: the same questions, the same dead ends, the same effort to make the memory whole when it would not come. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the burden of trying to understand why it had happened, frightened that she would remain trapped in these incomplete, alien pieces of memory, and hoping that treatment might help her bear the event without having to keep reliving it alone.
